In this module we will explore how to classify data into categories and reclassify existing categories. This is often a super important task when doing spatial analyses! Specifically, you will learn how to:

* Classify and reclassify objects using base R (`cut()`) and *stringr* and *dplyr* functions (both are **core tidyverse** packages);
* Create and modify factor data with the **core tidyverse** *forcats* package;
* Apply these techniques to spatial data.

*Note: Please continue to ignore references to the folder structure from our data science class.*

## Module overview

* **6.1 Categorizing data**: In this video lesson (runtime: 28:06) and written tutorial you will learn base R, *stringr*, and *dplyr* methods for classifying and reclassifying continuous and categorical data.
* **6.2 Factors are forcats**: This video lesson (runtime: 25:46) and compendium tutorial will really unlock the power of using the *forcats* package for classifying and reclassifying factors. I have spent the majority of my life trying to avoid factors ... with the *forcats* package I am all in!
* **6.3 Categorizing non-spatial and spatial data**: In this video lesson (runtime: 32:14) and written tutorial, we will learn how to apply our base R and tidyverse classification tools to shapefile and raster data!

**Problem Set** (due 5 Oct): Environmental equity

## Getting started

Please complete the following steps *prior* to beginning this week's lessons:

* Download [module_6_files.zip]{.mono} and:
    * Place the file [bird_cicadas_lc.rds]{.mono} inside of the [data/processed]{.mono} folder
    * Place the file [forcats_data.rds]{.mono} inside of the [data/raw]{.mono} folder
    * Place the R script files ([*.R]) inside of the [scripts]{.mono} folder 

***Important!***: *terra* will attempt to temporarily store raster files in your computer's memory. If it is unable to do so, it will store the data as a hidden temporary file on your hard drive Be sure to clear up enough space in your hard disk (at least 5 GB) to complete *terra* operations. If it is unable to store the file, you will get a very vague message about running out of memory (but this message actually has to do with running of hard disk space).

## About this week's data

This week we will use the following data files in our exercises:

[**birds_cicadas_lc.rds**]{.mono}:  This is a list object associated with a Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center study on a bird mortality event that occurred in 2021 (you can read about the event at [this link](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/suspect-list-narrows-in-mysterious-bird-die-off/){target="_blank"}). The data includes information on sick birds, cicada observations, and the land cover associated with each observation. The bird data are from a wildlife rescue agency in the District of Columbia, the land cover data were obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"}, and the cicada data were obtained from iNaturalist using the R package rinat.

[**canopy_cover.tif**]{.mono}:  This is geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the canopy cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by tree canopy.

[**dc_census.geojson**]{.mono}: This is a shapefile from the US Census Bureau that provides tract-level census data for the District of Columbia. The data were downloaded using the *tigris* and *tidycensus* packages in R.

[**dc_crimes.csv**]{.mono}: Crime data were obtained from <a href="https://opendata.dc.gov/" target="_blank">Open Data DC</a>. This is a tabular dataset and each row represents the record for an individual crime committed.

[**forcats_data.rds**]{.mono}:  This is a list object with example data that we will use in our forcats lesson. The list contains three character vectors and a small subset of the Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center’s banding data that we have used in the past.

[**impervious_surface.tif**]{.mono}: This is geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the impervious surface cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by man-made materials (e.g., pavement, sidewalks, rooftops).

[**nlcd.tif**]{.mono}: This is geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the land cover in the greater Washington DC region. Values are categorical and each value represents the dominant land cover class ([link](https://www.mrlc.gov/data/legends/national-land-cover-database-class-legend-and-description){target="_blank"}) of each cell.

[**sick_birds.geojson**]{.mono}: This is a point shapefile that represents sick birds that were brought to City Wildlife, a wildlife rehabilitation center in the District of Columbia, in the spring of 2021. These data were obtained directly from City Wildlife staff.
